1087453ea0f1cb: The C compiler is written in C. To build a new one, you use the previous one. That chain of “the old compiler builds the new one” is the point Thompson is going to exploit.
134a1011035b60: He modifies the compiler so that, when it detects it is compiling the login program, it secretly adds a master password. The login code looks clean; the binary already carries the backdoor.
1af0843e75e7ae: He teaches the compiler to recognize when it is compiling ITSELF and to insert both tricks again into the new compiler. It's a program that replicates inside its own build tool.
0c80a058dd51b6: Now he removes both tricks from the compiler's source code. They're no longer needed: the binary carries them and passes them on to every generation. Anyone reviewing the source code finds nothing unusual.
1871d10bc434d4: “You can't trust code that you did not totally create yourself.” Reviewing the source code isn't enough: you have to trust (or verify) the whole chain — compilers, tools and the people who made them. Today it's countered with reproducible builds and by compiling from several independent sources.
13c9f85e8ffe0b: Born on February 4, 1943 in New Orleans. He studied electrical engineering at the University of California, Berkeley (bachelor's 1965, master's 1966) and joined Bell Labs in 1966.
0af6d148e771e2: Together with Dennis Ritchie, he created Unix on a PDP-7 computer left unused after Bell Labs withdrew from the Multics project. Linux, macOS, Android and a good part of the Internet descend from it.
03706da5c9c7be: He wrote B, the direct ancestor of C (the language Ritchie developed from it).
07b3254b14d8b2: He brought regular expressions to text editors (ed) and created grep in 1973 to search for patterns in files: every security professional uses it today.
1ee42fec71ad30: With Joe Condon he built Belle, the world computer chess champion in 1980. Its endgame databases revolutionized computer chess.
0abe9c73bceaff: Co-author of Bell Labs' Plan 9. In 1992, with Rob Pike, he designed UTF-8 — the encoding that lets you write in any language and that almost the entire web uses today.
05b39ad5bba09c: At Google, with Robert Griesemer and Rob Pike, he designed the Go language, publicly presented in 2009.
0d788457afddd1: Turing Award 1983 (with Ritchie) · U.S. National Medal of Technology, 1998.
0b1e9be4ec7f09: In 2019, Thompson's Unix password from the 1970s, stored in the BSD source code, was cracked: it was “p/q2-q4!”, a chess move. Even his password was a pawn move.
1abd038b812afc: He is credited with the phrase: “When in doubt, use brute force”.
12a6c91530978a: His C language remains the foundation of operating systems, browsers and most security software.
10b00e73ec6d80: She created one of the first compilers and championed programming in something close to human language. She popularized the term “bug” after finding a moth in a Harvard computer in 1947.
0258a18ab9f4dc: In 1983 he started the free software movement: being able to read, modify and share code is a condition for being able to trust it.
049a3dc6900343: In 1991 he published the Linux kernel, now present in most of the world's servers and in Android.
01dcafd0b9ca16: In 1991 he published PGP so anyone could encrypt their email: privacy as a right.
157d7d86bec1ce: Famous for social engineering: he showed that tricking a person is often easier than breaking a machine.
03e549bcea7d10: Thompson's Turing Award lecture: the attack you can't see by reading the code. Walk through it step by step.
076f853506d13e: The people who built and broke the digital world — and from whom we are still learning. Each induction brings their story, their legacy and their security lesson.
0831b4dcea087c: If a compiler can hide a backdoor that appears in no source code, who do you trust when you install a program? What would you do to verify it?
